reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a cryptocurrency mining-pool opportunity that solicits payment for mining-related shares and uses tiered or team-based commissions tied to credited cryptocurrency earnings. It claims that greater investment can produce greater returns, including a possibility of making $400 with less investment, and shows a saved Bitcoin payout address and registration prompt. The separate LocalBitcoins screen is only an exchange demonstration, and the video does not show completed withdrawals, participant losses, or verified delivery of the advertised returns.

citations.quote: I bought the small most small pool I bought for 500 dollars
everything that is mined and everything that I get from marketing marketing results shows everything here
every day there is a calculation
everything that is mine goes to my wallet

opening.argument: The speaker presents a limited personal account, not a guarantee of universal profit. She expressly says, "I am not an investor" and explains that she purchased the minimum pool rather than claiming special expertise or certainty. Her results are described as an example of what happened to her, with the account showing only a small amount associated with that modest purchase. That framing encourages viewers to understand the opportunity through an individual experience and to assess the details themselves, rather than treating the presentation as a promise that everyone will earn money.

citations.quote: I am not an investor I did not have some kind of free at the time of join the company in large amounts
I bought a minimum minimum I bought a pool
that is, it's a penny this one yes

rebuttal.rebuttal: The existence of a $500 purchase and mining terminology does not by itself establish deception. The speaker disclosed that this was a minimum personal purchase and showed the account history rather than presenting an abstract promise. The prosecution also concedes that the video does not show participant losses or verified failure, so its conclusion depends on treating an openly displayed personal example as proof of a scam.

citations.quote: I bought the small most small pool I bought for 500 dollars
I am not an investor

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the purchase personal and small does not make the underlying offer safe. The presentation still connects payment for a pool with recurring mining credits and tells viewers that greater investment can produce greater returns. The speaker's modest starting amount is only a testimonial; it does not verify that the displayed credits are withdrawable, that returns are sustainable, or that viewers face comparable conditions.

citations.quote: The more you invest, the more can you get back
every day there is a calculation

opening.argument: The video's central activity is a walkthrough of how a logged-in account works. The speaker says she will show her personal office, identifies the mining figures, opens the pool, explains the wallet allocation, and promises a separate explanation of marketing. That is instructional demonstration and commentary on an unfamiliar cryptocurrency interface, not proof that viewers are being deceived. Showing where figures appear and how a user can change reinvestment settings is operational information; it leaves viewers able to inspect the process instead of asking them to accept an unsupported claim.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A tutorial format does not neutralize the subject matter, but the prosecution must still show that the speaker is making a deceptive solicitation. The video explains account screens, mining entries, and wallet settings, while its own opening admits that it does not establish completed withdrawals or participant losses. Those omissions leave a demonstration of account operation, not established scam conduct.

citations.quote: I will now show you some of the important moments
this is mining

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is not neutral software training: it teaches viewers how a paid mining pool is represented as producing recurring income and how marketing credits appear in the same account. The speaker explicitly says she bought a pool, and the displayed account contains mining-pool earnings and share information. Explaining an interface can still function as promotion when the demonstrated product is the investment opportunity itself.

citations.quote: I bought the small most small pool I bought for 500 dollars
everything that is mined and everything that I get from marketing marketing results shows everything here

opening.argument: The material can be understood as a service and account-use presentation, with separate discussion of how cryptocurrency may be exchanged for ordinary expenses. The speaker identifies a practical exchange resource and says she will demonstrate how she uses it. Crucially, the supplied material does not establish a guaranteed return, a demand for credentials, or proof that viewers must recruit others to recover a deposit. A visible wallet address and transaction history show account configuration and recorded entries, not by themselves a fraudulent mechanism.

citations.quote: there is a localbitcoin. One of the options is that you can buy and sell bitcoins here
It is a convenient resource where I'm using and I'm going to show you how I'm doing it

rebuttal.rebuttal: The account screens and a separate bitcoin exchange are consistent with ordinary cryptocurrency commerce. The prosecution identifies no stolen funds, false identity, credential harvesting, or completed withdrawal failure. Its reference to a tiered marketing explanation does not establish that the depicted service is fraudulent, especially where the speaker says the details will be explained in another video rather than presenting a hidden mechanism as fact.

citations.quote: there is a localbitcoin. One of the options is that you can buy and sell bitcoins here

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The exchange screen is separate from the paid mining offer and cannot validate it. The video still links a $500 pool purchase to daily mining calculations, and it describes marketing levels and commissions. A saved payout address proves only that an address was entered; it does not prove that the advertised mining returns were delivered or that the underlying service was legitimate.
